<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but A's pressure questions did real work: forcing B to name a concrete number ("one quarter of marquee fixtures") that B itself had already conceded targets the highest-demand, highest-premium inventory. A then used that concession repeatedly and effectively, framing B's revenue answer ("spending choices," "advertising can replace part of the fee") as an unquantified hope rather than a mechanism. B's access argument (live viewing matters, highlights aren't a substitute, free-to-air doesn't require a subscription-style recurring cost) remained intuitively strong and was never fully neutralized, but B's funding rebuttal stayed vague through both rebuttals and the closing, never specifying what "other spending" could realistically absorb a premium loss concentrated in the sport's most valuable games. A's closing crystallized this as "guaranteed cost vs. unguaranteed, already-substitutable benefit," which was the cleaner framing left standing after the exchange. Both A1/A2 and Q1/Q2 formats were followed correctly by both sides, so no format penalty applies. B's case had real appeal but the financial mechanism gap, repeatedly pressed and not closed, is the deciding weakness.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Questions (Turn 6), which forced B to name "one quarter of marquee fixtures" in Rebuttal 2 and thereby confirm A's earlier claim that the carve-out would target the highest-exclusivity-premium games — a concession A then leveraged through both remaining speeches while B's funding-mechanism response stayed abstract.</best_rebuttal>
